extracted.subtask_description: Preparing, editing, and distributing a Project Gutenberg edition of a public-domain work (here, Benjamin Franklin's Memoirs), including transcription fidelity, crediting, and compliance with the Project Gutenberg License.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transcriber's fidelity and correction notes
rubrics_metrics.description: Every effort has been made to replicate this text as faithfully as possible, including obsolete and variant spellings and other inconsistencies. Text that has been changed to correct an obvious error is noted at the end of this ebook.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve original orthography and variants except where an obvious error is corrected; any such corrections must be explicitly documented (e.g., noted at the end of the eBook).

rubrics_metrics.name: Credit and attribution for preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: Credits: E-text prepared by [names] and the Distributed Proofreading volunteers for Project Gutenberg.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When publishing the eBook, include credit lines for transcribers/proofreaders and mention Project Gutenberg and any volunteer groups involved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection criterion for collected works
rubrics_metrics.description: Selected with care from all his published productions, and comprising whatever is most entertaining and valuable to the general reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When compiling a collected edition, prioritize material considered entertaining and valuable to the general reader; selection should aim at readability and broad interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of industry (diligence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Industry is essential: idleness taxes many more than government taxes; 'If time be of all things the most precious, wasting time must be the greatest prodigality.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize practical maxims: avoid sloth, 'early to bed and early to rise', 'diligence is the mother of luck'; use concrete admonitions and aphorisms to promote steady work and productivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage and oversee your own affairs (steadiness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be steady, settled, and careful; oversee your own affairs with your own eyes and not trust too much to others—'The eye of a master will do more work than both his hands.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocate personal oversight of business and caution against overreliance on others; exemplify with proverbs and short anecdotes showing consequences of neglect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frugality and saving
rubrics_metrics.description: Frugality is necessary to make industry successful: avoid little expenses ('Many a little makes a mickle'), beware of extravagance, and 'If you would be wealthy, think of saving as well as of getting.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stress avoidance of small, habitual expenditures; illustrate with memorable sayings ('A small leak will sink a great ship') and comparisons between appearance and true prosperity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid running into debt
rubrics_metrics.description: Running into debt gives another power over your liberty; 'The second vice is lying, the first is running in debt.' Creditors have better memories than debtors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warn strongly against using credit for superfluities; counsel preferring to go without rather than incur debt, and highlight moral and practical consequences of indebtedness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use leisure productively
rubrics_metrics.description: Leisure is time for doing something useful; the diligent man will obtain leisure, but the lazy man never.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate leisure as earned time for useful activity versus mere idleness; advise planning and using spare time for constructive pursuits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation of reliance on personal effort; charity and humility
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not depend too much upon your own industry, frugality, and prudence; ask for the blessing of Heaven and be charitable to those who now seem to want it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance practical self-help advice with humility and charity; recommend aiding the needy and recognizing limits of personal control.

rubrics_metrics.name: True happiness arises from virtue and order
rubrics_metrics.description: All true happiness can only result from order and virtue; when reason governs the passions the happiness is of the rational nature, otherwise it is low and imperfect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promote cultivation of reason over passion, indifference to worldly things, and an expectation of higher goods; present virtue as both the means to happiness and a guard against life's evils.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue preserves health
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtue prescribes temperance and such a regulation of our passions as is most conducive to the well-being of the animal economy; it is the best preservation of health.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argue that moral conduct (temperance, regulation of passions) has concrete physical and mental health benefits; use this as a practical reason to pursue virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competence requirement for public men: be informed
rubrics_metrics.description: A man desirous to govern must be useful and informed: know the revenue and expenses of the state, the strength of forces by sea and land, the condition of mines and agriculture, and other particulars before advising policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advise that candidates for public office must have specific, practical knowledge of the state's affairs (finance, defence, resources) and not rely on vague ambition or conjecture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove capability in private affairs before taking public trust
rubrics_metrics.description: One should be able to manage one's own family and affairs well before undertaking the care of a whole people; inability in private matters shows incapacity for public office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the standard of demonstrated competence in smaller responsibilities as a precondition for larger public duties; recommend gaining experience and success locally first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to serve if truly capable
rubrics_metrics.description: Conversely, those modest but capable persons (like Charmidas) are obliged as citizens to take care of the commonwealth and should not decline public employment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cast public service as a civic obligation for competent citizens; encourage accepting public roles when one is fit to serve for the common good.
